19739-modern-american-prose-selections:
Modern American Prose Selections, dated 1909, gathers American writing for study and reading. One piece marks the hundredth anniversary of a great American's birth. The speaker calls him one of the two greatest Americans. He ranks him among the two or three greatest men of the nineteenth century. That centenary was Abraham Lincoln's, widely celebrated in 1909.

School anthologies shaped what counted as American prose. Editors chose speeches, essays, and addresses that modeled clear writing. Lincoln pieces anchored many such collections. Students learned style by reading masters aloud. The book preserves that classroom canon in one binding. It shows which voices teachers trusted in 1909. For literary history, the table of choices matters as much as the texts.
19798-the-farringdons:
Ellen Thorneycroft Fowler set The Farringdons in England's Black Country. One street in the novel faces two worlds at once. West-side houses have sunny gardens and orchards sloping to meadows. Eastward stand tall chimneys, weird and terrible yet fascinating. Beyond the fields rise the Clee Hills and the Wrekin. Blue Welsh mountains close the far distance.

Fowler's novels mixed industry, faith, and family ambition. The Farringdons are a clan shaped by that divided landscape. Money from furnaces meets conscience from chapel and garden. Her Black Country detail comes from living beside it. The book preserves a region literature often skipped. It does so with affection and a sharp eye.
19977-the-blue-pavilions:
The Blue Pavilions is a historical romance by Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch, writing as Q. It opens at Harwich on 11 October 1673, at noonday. More than a hundred tall ships have newly returned from the Dutch War. The little seaport beside the Stour presents a lively appearance. Quiller-Couch builds the scene with a painter's patience. War's end fills the harbor with noise and color.

Q wrote sea-soaked Cornish and naval tales under that single letter. The Dutch wars gave him a rich, neglected century. Pavilions are campaign tents; blue ones suggest the fleet's shore world. His prose is consciously beautiful, sentence by sentence. This novel shows his romantic history at full sail. It is a connoisseur's adventure story.
20083-a-boswell-of-baghdad-with-diversio:
A Boswell of Baghdad, With Diversions, takes its name from James Boswell, the famed life writer. The narrator faces a work in four huge volumes that could fell a bookseller. That joke sets a tone of wit, books, and talk. Baghdad gives the book its far-off, storied frame.

Diversions, in the old sense, are side trips and bright asides. The book mixes tale, essay, and chat about books and men. Its charm lies in voice more than in plot alone. Readers who like learned humor will find a rich, rambling companion here.
20137-a-comparative-view-of-religions:
Francis T. Washburn wrote A Comparative View of Religions, a study of the world's faiths. He sets out each faith and weighs it against the Christian one. True religion, he argues, was prepared in Israel and fulfilled in Christ. In Christ, man knows his oneness with God, he writes.

Washburn grants that Islam holds truth and good in its teachings. Yet he holds that such truth was borrowed from older faiths. The book shows how one Christian writer of his era ranked all faiths. Readers get a clear, dated map of comparative religion from that standpoint.
20459-hours-in-a-library-volume-1-new-ed:
Hours in a Library gathers literary essays by Leslie Stephen, the critic and editor who shaped Victorian letters. This is the first volume, in a new edition with additions. Stephen writes about authors as a fellow worker among books, not as a distant judge.

The volume opens with a famous daydream about an old library. It seems, he writes, as if the souls of all the writers who left their work to the Bodleian were resting there. He feels he inhales learning while walking its shelves. The essays that follow keep that mix of deep reading and plain talk.
20468-the-delta-of-the-triple-elevens: The Delta of the Triple Elevens preserves service records of a World War outfit. It lists men one by one, with dates and postings. One clerk went on detached service on May 18, 1918, at Camp Meade. He rejoined Battery D on June 27 and sailed with it to France. Such lines trace how a unit was built and sent overseas.
20487-shakspere-personal-recollections:
Shakspere: Personal Recollections is a whimsical satire that claims an impossible narrator. The writer says it is well known among his close friends that he is no ordinary man. He claims to have lived forever, and to be ready to recall Shakespeare in person.

He says he sprang from the race of Strulbugs, who live forever on the island of Immortality. That island lies on the coast of Japan, and he began there more than a million years ago. The tall tale riffs on Swift's deathless Struldbrugs, and uses the joke to mock solemn Shakespeare worship.
20614-the-wonder-island-boys-the-mysteri:
The Mysteries of the Caverns, published in 1914, carries Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys deeper into their island's secrets. The boys and their professor friend keep building a working life from wreckage and raw materials. Each chapter reads like a lesson disguised as an adventure.

The contents move from recovering the lifeboat to deciding to row it around the point. The boys study alloys and their uses, and make stocks for their guns. They begin the hull of a new boat, learning what shape a hull should take. Their tame charge, Red Angel, even attempts to whistle.
20838-the-infra-medians:
A hot sales prospect waits, but the narrator of The Infra-Medians runs to his buddy Vic instead. Vic is Hope's brother, and the two have been pals since childhood. Sewell Peaslee Wright drops that bond into a tale of hidden beings.

Wright wrote brisk science fiction for the pulp magazines of his day. Infra-medians, creatures between worlds, give this tale its strange hook. Fast talk, sudden peril, and weird science drive the plot. Readers of early pulp tales will find Wright's pace and invention on show, with friendship, not just wonder, at the tale's core.
20980-a-survey-of-russian-literature-wit:
Vladimir, Grand Prince of Kiev, took Christianity for his whole nation in 988, this survey recounts. Baptised wholesale from Byzantium, Russia gained its Prince-Saint in that act. His grandmother Olga had paved the way with churches in Kiev before him.

Isabel Hapgood surveys Russian writing from chronicles to the great novelists of her day. Her 1902 book adds chosen pieces in her own English versions. Hapgood knew Russia deeply and turned its classics with rare care. Readers get both a map of a vast literature and a taste of its goods, in one trusted guide.
21044-the-willoughby-captains:
School parliament reports tangle speakers, teller, and heckling boys in The Willoughby Captains, Reed owns. The printed book simplifies what his tale tries to render by rule. That frank note fronts a reissue of Talbot Baines Reed's school classic.

Captains of house and games rule Willoughby's boy world in this tale. Honour, rivalry, and a disputed place drive its famed plot along. Reed helped invent the modern school story with books like this one. Willoughby's boys still feel alive: vain, brave, funny, and bound by codes they would die sooner than break in public.
21243-the-madigans:
Miriam Michelson's 1904 story collection follows the Madigan girls of San Francisco through ten linked tales. The first, Cecilia the Pharisee, opens with Sissy feeling virtuous before she has done anything at all. Other stories include A Pagan and a Puritan, The Shut-Ups, and The Ancestry of Irene.

Irene and her many supposed fathers appear in Orson Lowell's illustrations, including the frontispiece. The sisters scheme, pretend, write letters, and manage their widowed household with more wit than money. Michelson had written In the Bishop's Carriage, and she gives the Madigans the same quick talk and warm disorder. Kate: A Pretense and Old Mother Gibson close the set.
21244-by-canoe-and-dog-train-among-the-c:
Egerton Ryerson Young was a Hamilton pastor, newly married, when a letter from the Mission Rooms in Toronto reached his study in 1868. The Missionary Committee asked him to go as a missionary to the Indigenous peoples at Norway House in the Northwest. His memoir tells how he answered that summons.

Young travelled by canoe, dog train, and prairie trail toward Hudson Bay country, among the Cree and Saulteaux peoples named in his title. Chapters record frontier settlers, Sioux wars, and narrow escapes on the way. The book became a well-known record of Canadian Methodist mission life in the early Northwest, told by the man who lived it.
21315-the-king-s-sons:
King Ethelwulf of Wessex had four sons, and each in turn became king. George Manville Fenn's short tale follows the brothers, above all the youngest, Alfred, later Alfred the Great. Their tutor is Father Swythe, a monk, and only Alfred cares for what he teaches. The others prefer rougher pursuits.

Fenn pauses the story for a fine lesson in how illuminated manuscripts were made: the inks, the colours, the pens and brushes. Father Swythe later becomes Bishop Swithun of Winchester, whose feast day still carries a forty-days-of-rain legend. This quiet volume trades Fenn's usual cliffhangers for early English history told simply for young readers.
21316-the-adventures-of-don-lavington-no:
Lindon Lavington, called Don, works as a clerk in his uncle Josiah's Bristol sugar and tobacco office and hates the work. When office money goes missing, the real thief is plain to see, yet Uncle Josiah keeps accusing Don. George Manville Fenn then takes the boy's life apart in one night.

Don and Jem, a fellow worker who has also quarrelled at home, go out feeling ill-used and are seized by a press gang. They escape their ship in New Zealand, live among Maori friends, and help English settlers fight off an attack stirred by escaped convicts. In the end one villain proves to be the office thief all along.
21330-robert-burns:
Principal Shairp, professor of poetry at Oxford, wrote this life of Robert Burns. It was first published in 1879 and many times reprinted; this edition is from 1906. Eight chapters run from Burns's youth in Ayrshire through his two Edinburgh winters, his Border and Highland tours, and his farm at Ellisland. The move to Dumfries and the last years follow.

A closing chapter weighs Burns's character, poems, and songs together. Shairp notes that six biographies of Burns had already appeared before Carlyle's famous essay of 1828, and the count only grew. His own life stays compact and readable, aimed at students meeting Scotland's national poet in one volume.
21368-the-silver-canyon-a-tale-of-the-we:
Bart is a young hero out on the western plains with his uncle. In the middle of the nineteenth century, in George Manville Fenn's tale, he is seeking a new life. Antelope steaks cook over a dying fire as dangers gather: armed Native warriors skilled at creeping up unseen, rattlesnakes, and bears. The party finds a great rocky hill with a rich lode of silver in it.

The hill was mined long before, perhaps thousands of years earlier, and its summit gives grazing and a strong defensive post. They work the remaining ore commercially while attacks continue almost to the end. A railway at last reaches the mine, and a town of thousands follows the silver.
21443-vesty-of-the-basins:
Sarah P. McLean Greene sets her 1892 novel Vesty of the Basins in a small fishing village on the coast. A low, storm-beaten schoolhouse, a stranded schooner, and a fog horn mark the place. The horn was the gift of Melchias Tibbitts, a dead captain of the Basin.

Vesty's tale moves through meetings, courtship, a wedding, and village feasts. Captain Leezur's sly wooing and tall tales give the book much of its fun. Greene writes the local speech with a loving, exact ear. Her earlier Cape Cod Folks had made her name for just this kind of coastal portrait.
21459-dick-onslow-among-the-redskins:
Dick Onslow joins a party of emigrants bound for California in W. H. G. Kingston's Dick Onslow. The tale ranges in and near the Rocky Mountains, on the hard road west. Dick's friend, meanwhile, tells of cutting his way through Mexico and the settled States.

Rattlesnakes, bears, rockslides, and snow slides crowd the trail. Raids by hostile tribes bring shots, wounds, and nights spent hiding in bush and tree. Dick is shot through the leg and starves in sight of plenty. The book is not long, but Kingston packs each chapter with peril drawn from backwoods life.
21466-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Ralph and Clarice, brother and sister, lose both parents on the road west in W. H. G. Kingston's In the Rocky Mountains. Their farming family had left the middle states for a new life. Orphaned, the two young folk have no adult to lead them on.

A wagon train then comes by, and its chief proves to be their own uncle Jeff Crockett. Uncle Jeff never could abide folk crowding round his hut, and always moved on. He takes the children in and becomes dear to them. Clashes with Indigenous peoples, wolves, and bears fill the rest of this short, warm tale.
21739-hunting-the-lions:
Tom Brown, a hero with the plainest name in England, leads this Ballantyne hunting tale. Ballantyne spends his first chapter joking about the Browns of the world: grocers, butchers, milkmen, and doctors beyond counting. Then he takes his own Brown far from those safe streets.

The trail leads to lion country, where hunting tests nerve in a way no shop counter can. Ballantyne builds the tale on travel, camp life, and the charge of a lion at close range. His humor about the hero's name keeps the tone light between dangers. It is a sporting yarn of his classic kind, written for boys who dreamed of Africa from an English fireside.
21763-the-brentons:
Young Scott Brenton is led into the ministry by his widowed mother's secret prayers in this 1912 novel by Anna Chapin Ray. The prayer was never made to him, the narrator insists, but offered in silence and sincerity. Scott's path into the church gives the family of the title its center. Around him, the Brentons face the pulls of duty, love, and pride.

Ray was a practiced novelist of family life, with many titles to her name by 1912. Her touch here is quiet and close, following talk across tables and the small turns that change lives. The frontispiece shows young Catia in talk over a cup. It is a gentle book about faith tested inside a household.
21771-georgina-s-reasons:
Raymond Benyon loves a girl he cannot understand in this Henry James tale of 1885, and he knows it from the start. Georgina is tall and fair, with gorgeous auburn hair and a cold, beautiful eye. Her charm is real, yet Benyon feels a twinge of warning even in his happiness. Her parents are rude to him, and her singularity takes forms he cannot name.

James follows the love affair through its happy surface and its hidden cracks. Georgina has her reasons, and the tale's work is to bring them slowly into view. Benyon looks back in later years and calls his early unease a foreboding. It is a cool, exact study of a woman who will not be read like other people.
21903-the-californians:
Old California families collide with new American wealth in Gertrude Atherton's novel The Californians, published in 1898. Helena Belmont, sixteen and spoiled, tips her schoolbooks to the floor and demands the sun. Her dark-eyed friend Magdaléna Yorba has only her intelligence to set against Helena's beauty and money. Miss Phelps, their teacher, leaves the quarrel to Miss Yorba, as the opening scene jokes.

Atherton, a Californian herself, writes the passing of the Spanish dons' world with an insider's eye. Helena already knows the power of wealth, and sparkles with the insolence of it. Love, pride, and race run through the tale of the two girls. It is early Atherton: sharp, scenic, and set on showing California to readers who knew only its gold-rush face.
21931-sea-urchins:
Dockside boys and old sailors fill Sea Urchins, W. W. Jacobs's book of tales from 1899. The first story, Smoked Skipper, opens with a porter trotting a bran-new sea-chest toward Wapping Old Stairs. Its owner, a small ill-looking lad of fourteen, swears there is little about the sea he does not know. He orders his hellum turned with a captain's airs while the porter plays along for a cheap half-crown.

Other tales bring a grey parrot, a lost ship, pickled herring, and brother Hutchins. Jacobs writes the London river as a comedy stage where everyone is slightly at sea. The dialect is thick and the timing perfect. Sea Urchins catches his world young: urchins, skippers, and the men who carry their chests and their illusions.
21996-riviera-towns:
Hill towns above the French Riviera are walked one by one in Herbert Adams Gibbons's Riviera Towns, with Lester George Hornby's illustrations, copyrighted in 1920. From his study window at Théoule, Gibbons could almost count the windows of distant houses. Grasse on its hill was a constant temptation, and the two islands offshore kept watch. His chapters visit Cagnes, Saint-Paul, Vence, and Menton before the famous coast towns.

Monte Carlo, Villefranche, Nice, Antibes, and Cannes each get a chapter, with Mougins, Fréjus, and Saint-Raphaël to close. Gibbons looks past the casinos to old streets, courts where stables stood downstairs, and meadows thick with violets. The book was dedicated to Helen and Margaret, who indulged author and artist both. It is travel writing with a resident's patience.
22083-myths-and-legends-of-the-great-pla:
Katharine Berry Judson gathered Myths and Legends of the Great Plains in 1913. Judson made a career of collecting Native tales for general readers. The Plains peoples here include the Kiowa, Pawnee, Osage, and their neighbours. Their stories explain the buffalo, the stars, the seasons, and the spirit world.

One plate shows a dreamer priest's vision of the land of the dead. He crosses a prairie crowded with buffalo and ponies to find his dead brothers. Creation tales, trickster stories, and war stories stand side by side. Judson aimed to keep these tales in print for readers who would never hear a tribal storyteller. The book reflects both the tales and her era.
22220-policing-the-plains:
R. G. MacBeth wrote Policing the Plains as the real-life record of the Royal North-West Mounted Police. MacBeth, author of The Romance of Western Canada, tells the Mounties' story from their founding march west in 1874. The frontispiece shows mounted police rounding up horse thieves. The force's work was exactly that: patrol, pursue, and keep order across an immense frontier.

MacBeth follows famous marches, whisky traders, Sitting Bull's arrival, and the North-West Rebellion. He writes as an admirer, and the book is a celebration. Published in the 1920s, it fixed the Mountie legend for a generation. Here was the red coat who always got his man. He ruled the plains with a handful of riders.
22362-appreciations-and-criticisms-of-th:
Appreciations and Criticisms of the Works of Charles Dickens gathers judgments on England's great novelist. After Dickens fell ill and died, a school of criticism arose. It held, oddly, that a man wrote better when he was ill.

George Gissing, an able writer, nearly argued that Little Dorrit is Dickens's best book. That claim shows the strange turns Dickens criticism took. The volume sorts praise and blame across his career. Readers can watch taste change as distance from Dickens grew. It suits anyone who wants the arguments around the novels, not only the novels themselves, preserved in period voices.
22767-pagan-passions:
Pagan Passions is a science fiction novel of 1959. In it, the gods and goddesses of Olympus return to a modern world. Their return greatly inconveniences a man named Forrester. The catalog record names no author. Its own billing gives the recipe plainly: gods, intrigue, mystery, and danger, with the supernatural made to make sense.

For science fiction it is, the blurb insists, with the supernatural made logical, and fun too, despite the sword that hangs by a thread above Forrester's head. Divine politics, played as suspense comedy, drives the plot: old gods with old grudges, armed with very modern leverage. The book belongs to the bright, cheeky school of late-1950s science fiction, when the field delighted in dressing myth in a business suit.
22892-the-best-made-plans:
Everett B. Cole opens The Best Made Plans with a camera's eye sweeping a future city. It centers on a large sports stadium where players dash across the turf, then swings away over city scenes. The view then crosses the palace walls and drops to the Royal Guards' parade ground.

That cool, surveying gaze suits a story about schemes inside a polished state. Plans here are made by rulers and plotters alike, and the title warns how the best of them go. Cole wrote workmanlike science fiction for the magazines, strong on setting and mechanism. Readers get a future court, a watching lens, and intrigue that unfolds at a steady clip.
23066-the-prairie-traveler-a-hand-book-f:
Randolph B. Marcy offers hard-won knowledge in The Prairie Traveler, his handbook for overland expeditions. The information is so varied, and drawn from so many sources, he writes, that every new expedition still adds to his practical knowledge. A sound prairie manual, Marcy is convinced, belongs in every young traveler's kit, worth more than its weight many times over.

Marcy, an army officer, wrote the West's most trusted guidebook for the wagon and saddle era. Routes between the Mississippi and the Pacific, water, grass, camps, and encounters fill its chapters. Emigrants carried it like a spare wheel. Modern readers find in it the whole logistics of westward travel, exact, unromantic, and quietly lifesaving.
23169-the-diamond-lens:
Fitz-James O'Brien buys a microscope in The Diamond Lens. The promised instrument arrives at last, a simple Field's microscope costing perhaps fifteen dollars. For teaching purposes, the narrator judges, no better apparatus could have been chosen. A small treatise on microscopy, its history and discoveries, came with it.

From that schoolboy instrument O'Brien builds his famous tale of obsession. A diamond lens, a world within a water drop, and a beauty beyond reach complete it. Written in 1858, it stands near the head of American science fiction. The fifteen-dollar microscope does real work in the telling, grounding the wonder in a boy's budget. Every later story of microscopic worlds descends from this drop.
23261-oowikapun-or-how-the-gospel-reache:
Oowikapun tells how the gospel reached the Nelson River Indians, through the life of a young Indigenous hunter. His simple, quiet, monotonous life is broken in upon in a way he cannot undo. He can never be the same again after what reaches him.

A decided awakening has come. The circle of his vision has suddenly widened, and he has become aware that he is something more than he had imagined. The tale is a missionary story told from inside that change of mind. Readers get a period account of faith arriving in a northern hunting community, and of one young man's response.
a-lady-s-life-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Isabella L. Bird wrote these letters to her sister during a long ride through the Colorado Rockies, when the region was still rough frontier. She travels by train and on horseback past Lake Tahoe and Utah mining towns, then into mountain boarding houses and lonely log camps. An introduction by Ann Ronald opens this edition.

Letter by letter she records grizzly bears, snow, bad roads, rough settlers, and grand peaks, along with climbs and long solo rides. She notices both hardship and beauty, and she writes with humor about her own dress and manners. The letters remain a lively record of the mountain West seen by a bold English traveler.
a-rogue-s-life-by-wilkie-collins:
A Rogue's Life, published in 1856, is a short novel by Wilkie Collins, the early master of mystery and suspense who later wrote The Woman in White and The Moonstone. Collins tells the tale as a picaresque, following the fortunes of an endearing young man named Frank Softly. It is a story of thwarted ambition and forbidden love, told with a wink.

Frank's ever-hopeful father pushes him into society and tries him in one profession after another, hoping something will stick. Frank's own take on each attempt keeps the narrative comic and quick. Early Collins is on display here: entertaining, loosely plotted around scrapes and romance, and already skilled at holding a reader through a rogue's confession.
a-shepherd-s-life-impressions-of-the-sou:
W. H. Hudson wrote A Shepherd's Life from time spent on the South Wiltshire Downs, and a note records that one chapter began as articles in Longman's Magazine in 1902. The country is Salisbury Plain and the Wylye valley, and the people are the shepherds, villagers, poachers, and sheep-dogs of a chalk-down farming world already passing away when he wrote.

At the center stands shepherd Isaac Bawcombe, whose talk, Bible reading, fox lore, and early memories fill many chapters. Around him Hudson sets bird life on the downs, deer-stealers, sheep-bells, old Wiltshire days, and the hard economics of a shepherd's family. The book is part memoir, part oral history, and part naturalist's notebook, all in Hudson's plain, lingering style.
a-tale-of-three-lions:
H. Rider Haggard opens with Allan Quatermain back in the wilderness, unable to bear civilization's crowds for long, as old hunters seldom can. The first chapter, The Interest on Ten Shillings, sets up a debt owed and a story owed with it. Quatermain pays in the coin he has: a hunting tale.

Three chapters carry the party after lions, to what was found in the pool, and to Jim-Jim's revenge. Haggard writes the hunts with a sportsman's exactness about rifles, ground, and lion behavior, learned in his own African years. The tale is short, told in camp style, and it shows Quatermain's world before the great romances made him famous.
a-treatise-on-the-six-nation-indians:
J. B. Mackenzie presents his treatise as a lecture preserved without change, as his preface says, on the Six-Nation Indians, the Iroquois league of Canada and New York. A prefatory note corrects his own earlier wording about the Indian writer Peter Jones, an attempt at fairness that sets the book's tone. The league's members were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and Tuscarora.

Mackenzie describes the confederacy's councils, sachems, clan system, wampum records, and laws, and its long history of war and diplomacy with French, English, and Americans. He writes as a Canadian observer of his own century. The treatise is a compact period account of one of the strongest Indigenous political unions in North America.
a-waif-of-the-plains:
Bret Harte sees the Great Plains first through the eyes of two children in a hooded emigrant wagon in the summer of 1852. Dust, heat, the smell of cattle, and a low dark line that never changes shape: that is the world of Clarence and Susy, traveling west with a wagon train. When trouble strikes the train, the children are left to the plains.

Eleven chapters carry the waifs through hunger, rescue, and new homes among soldiers and settlers. Harte writes the crossing with a child's-eye plainness that makes the dangers sharper. The tale is one of his tenderest Western stories, balancing the cruelty of abandonment against the kindness of strangers.
actions-and-reactions:
Actions and Reactions, published in 1909, is a collection of short stories by Rudyard Kipling. Kipling, author of The Jungle Book and Kim, gathered here a set of tales from the later part of his career. The best known of them, With the Night Mail, imagines a future world of airships carrying the mail across the night sky.

Around that vision stand stories of England, empire, and ordinary work, each in Kipling's manner answered by a companion poem. The collection's title states its physics: every act in these tales draws a consequence after it. It shows Kipling in his mature short form, mixing invention, craft, and moral pressure in compact stories.
air-service-boys-in-the-big-battle-or-si:
Charles Amory Beach opens near the airdromes outside Paris. Sergeant Tom Raymond lies on a cot in his tent there. His chum Jack Parmly teases him in the slang the boys picked up from French comrades. Bad news from the air starts the tale. The contents promise a girl's appeal, anxious waiting, and transfer to the American front.

Twenty-five chapters follow Tom and Jack through a battle in the air. Stunts, flights over the lines, a perfect shot, and a daring scheme follow. A crash comes before the mission of the subtitle: silencing the big guns. Beach wrote boys' aviation adventure while the Great War still raged, and his heroes fly for the new American air service.
among-the-tibetans:
Isabella Bird's Among the Tibetans records her ride into Ladakh, the high desert the maps called Little Tibet. She travels from Kashmir over the passes to Leh, the Indus valley capital, in 1889. Her pages fill with what the road offered: Buddhist monasteries on cliffs, lamas at their prayers, prayer wheels, and villages farmed at altitudes where barley barely ripens. Bird, the indefatigable Victorian traveler of Persia and the Rockies, rides with her servant and her notebook through country few Europeans had described.

The book is short and dense: customs, funerals, polyandry, and the great monastery of Hemis pass in quick, exact sketches. She admires the Tibetans' cheerfulness in a climate that kills gardens. Readers get Bird in miniature here: an empire of observation in one summer's ride. It is a portrait of Ladakhi life before the roads came.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
John McElroy, late of Company L, 16th Illinois Cavalry, tells what he lived through as a Union prisoner. His title page of 1879 names the prisons. They are Richmond, Andersonville, Savannah, Millen, Blackshear, and Florence. Fifteen months a guest of the so-called Southern Confederacy, he calls it, with bitter humor. The book is dedicated to Justice Noah Swayne of the Supreme Court.

Eighty-two chapters follow capture, the stockade at Andersonville, hunger, disease, the dead line, exchange, and release. McElroy writes as a private soldier, naming comrades and guards alike. His account became the most widely read Northern prison memoir, and its anger and detail still make it hard, necessary reading about the Civil War.
b09-luther-hymns:
Martin Luther wrote hymns as well as tracts, and the songs may have carried his cause furthest of all. The hymns here, Deutsche Geistliche Lieder, begin in 1524, when his first songbooks appeared. Among them stands A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, still sung around the world.

German texts stand with English versions, and the tunes are printed with the words. Leonard Woolsey Bacon edited the set in 1884 for singers and scholars alike. Luther held that music drives out sorrow and teaches faith to the young. These pages show the Reformation as people actually sang it, in church, school, and home.
bandelier-hemenway-contributions:
Bandelier wrote his Contributions for the Hemenway Expedition, and they appeared in 1890. The Swiss-American scholar rebuilt the Southwest's written past from the archives. Pueblo and Spanish colonial history had never been traced with such care.

Dusty records in Mexico yield towns, missions, and peoples long lost. Bandelier sorts true reports from myth and mere boast by hard proof. His pages trace how Spain entered the region and what it found. Later digs and studies across the Southwest rest on this base. The book remains bedrock for the region's early history in print. Its notes still guide researchers through the archives today.
brewster-s-millions:
George Barr McCutcheon's Brewster's Millions begins at a birthday dinner of the Little Sons of the Rich. Monty Brewster, a clean-looking young bank clerk, is the company favourite. His grandfather, Edwin Peter Brewster, was many times a millionaire. Monty expects a comfortable inheritance and little else.

A first will leaves him a million dollars outright. A second will, from a forgotten uncle, offers seven millions more on one condition. Monty must spend the first million within a year, show nothing for it, and keep the secret. Chapters follow his splendid waste through yachts, operas, and a rescued heroine named Peggy. The promise of thrift ends the game at the last hour. McCutcheon wrote the perfect spending fantasy, later beloved on stage and screen.
california-and-the-californians:
David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University, wrote California and the Californians as a short essay of interpretation. The Californian, he begins, loves a state that loves him back. Outside criticism, however aimed, flies wide of the mark. Yet Californians may say hard things about themselves that strangers may not.

Jordan lists the charges cheerfully: sleepy commerce, gambling industries, shabbiness, and saloon politics. Then he answers them from the land itself. Scenery, climate, and freedom of life are the three sources of California's charm. From Siskiyou to San Diego he surveys missions, sierras, valleys, and surf. The essay is brief, fifty pages of prose, and reads as a founding president's defence of his adopted state against Eastern condescension.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leri:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Lérins describes an island monastery off Provence, on Saint-Honorat island, a league off Provence's coast. St. Honoratus founded it early in the fifth century, living first as a hermit before followers gathered from Roman Gaul and Brittany alike.

Through the fifth, sixth and seventh centuries Lérins exerted considerable influence, until Saracen raids made monkish life unworkable or shaky for two hundred years. Restored in the eleventh century, the abbey gained estates, churches and privileges from popes, counts of Provence and kings of France. Its monks also defended the coast against Moorish incursions from Algeria through the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Albans describes a Hertfordshire abbey. Offa, King of the Mercians, founded it about 793. Bede, writing early in the eighth century, already speaks of a church of wonderful workmanship, fine enough for the martyrdom it honoured. Offa's monastery grew beside that church, which he repaired with papal approval.

Willegod, the king's kinsman, became abbot, and by 1000 the old church again stood dilapidated. Abbots Ealdred and Eadmer gathered materials from Roman Verulam's ruins, and Abbot Paul of Caen began the new church in 1077, completing the whole in eleven years. Adrian the Fourth later freed St. Albans from bishops' control and ranked it first among English abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedarians:
The Abecedarians were a sect of Anabaptists who scorned all human learning, holding that God enlightens his chosen people inwardly and gives them needed truth through visions and ecstasies. They rejected every other path to knowledge and claimed that salvation required ignorance even of the first letters of the alphabet, which gave the group its name. Study of theology struck them as a kind of idolatry, and they treated learned preachers as men who falsified God's word.

In 1522 Nicholas Storch and Zwickau's prophets began preaching this teaching at Wittenberg, mixed with other errors. Carlstadt was drawn to it and put it into practice so fully that he surrendered his doctoral title to work as a street porter. For a while he preached the new teaching to Wittenberg's people and students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-janss:
Abraham Janssens was a Flemish painter born at Antwerp about 1573 who probably died there about 1631. Also known as Janssens van Nuyssen, he likely took that name from his mother's family to set himself apart from other artists named Janssens. He was a pupil of Jan Snellinck and entered the Guild of St. Luke as a teaching master in 1601. He married the next year and raised a family, and his daughter Anna married Jan Breughel the younger.

Houbraken started a story that Janssens bitterly opposed Rubens, but his work is the only authority for that legend. The entry judges Houbraken hostile to Janssens. In fact Janssens was a respected contemporary of Rubens, spoken of warmly by fellow artists in Antwerp. In colour's splendour and composition's vigour, only Rubens surpassed him in his day, and many of his pictures were engraved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acclamation-i:
Acclamation is one of three valid forms of papal election, alongside scrutiny and compromise. The method rests on the constitutions of Gregory XV, confirmed by Urban VIII. Acclamation, also called quasi-inspiration, consists in all cardinals present unanimously proclaiming one candidate Supreme Pontiff without casting votes. Since it must happen without prior consultation or negotiation, it is viewed as proceeding from the Holy Ghost.

Recent examples anchor the account. Clement X, formerly Cardinal Altieri, was elected in 1670 after the crowd outside the conclave cried Altieri Papa, a cry the cardinals confirmed. Innocent XI, elected in 1676, was surrounded in the conclave chapel and, despite his resistance, had every cardinal kiss his hand and proclaim him pope. The entry cites Ferraris, Wernz, De Montor, and Keller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-roman:
Acts of Roman Congregations is the term for documents, also called decrees, issued by the Roman Congregations under powers conferred by the pope. The entry treats the subject under six heads: kinds, authority, use, manner of preservation, accessibility, and collections. In kinds, these bodies grant privileges and dispensations, issue ordinances, give true readings of law, and decide cases between contending parties, though not every body holds all these powers.

Decrees are for single cases or church-wide, by whether they address individuals or the whole church, and most deal with discipline, explaining, enforcing, or dispensing from positive church laws. Some deal with doctrine, declaring a doctrine untenable or an act unlawful against divine law. In authority, these decrees are supreme in a sense, coming from the highest church tribunals, but not wholly supreme, since the Congregations are distinct in law from the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-:
Advocates of Roman Congregations, ecclesiastical or lay, know canon and civil law and plead causes before Rome's ecclesiastical tribunals. The learning required is exceptional and profound. Beyond thorough jurisprudence, canonical and civil, they must know theology and history, sacred and profane. Frequent references to councils, canons, and papal decrees demand deep and varied learning covering languages ancient and modern.

A Roman advocate differs from an ordinary legal pleader in several ways. He does not establish facts in a case, since that is the procurator's business. He assumes the facts given him to be true and builds his legal argument on them, freed from tempting distortions of testimony. He pleads always before learned judges, not a jury, so his language must be sober, refined, clear, and precise. His fee is fixed, win or lose, and consistorial advocates must defend the poor free of charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeons:
Aeons is the term Gnostic heresiarchs used for spiritual powers arising by progressive emanation from the eternal Being. Together they form the Pleroma, the unseen spiritual world, as distinct from the Kenoma, the visible material world. The word aeon, aion, means age, the ever-existing, or eternity, and came to denote the divine eternal power and its personified attributes.

From there it extended to successive emanations from divinity, seen as needed links between spiritual and material worlds. The concept traces to a philosophy holding divinity incapable of contact with matter or evil. The wish was to square that view with Christian belief in God's direct action in creation and redemption. Jewish angelology and Hellenic systems of go-betweens suggested a series of lesser heavenly powers, each less perfect the further from the supreme deity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agents-of-rom:
Agents of Roman Congregations look after their patrons' affairs at the Roman Curia. The name comes from Latin Agens in Rebus, matching Greek Apocrisiarius. Such agents first appear not at Rome but at Constantinople's imperial palace. There bishops, given church and state's close tie and the lack of canons on mixed matters, needed men to watch their interests at court.

Until the French Revolution, French prelates kept like agents at St. Denis's royal court. Today bishops or private persons employ agents in the pontifical courts, temporarily or permanently. Their chief business is pressing patrons' cases forward. For favours such as dispensations they prepare supplications and call repeatedly on officials until an answer comes. They rank next before the notaries, and their pay rests wholly on employers' will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexian-nuns: The Alexian nuns, or black sisters, began early in the fifteenth century as religious women affiliated to the Alexian Brotherhood. They adopted the Rule of St. Augustine and took up the Brothers' bodily works of mercy. Their dress is black: a mantle of matching colour and a white cap gave them their common name. The black, or Cellitine, sisters now have their mother-house at Cologne, and they have no houses in the United States and Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexians:
The Alexians, also called Cellites, are a religious congregation that began at Mechlin in Brabant in the fifteenth century, during the ravages of the Black Death. Certain laymen joined under a man named Tobias to help the plague-stricken, without taking vows or adopting a rule at first. The institute took its name from St. Alexius, and its brothers devoted themselves to burying the dead and nursing the sick.

The Alexian Brothers run four hospitals in the United States. The first, built at Chicago in 1866, burned in the great fire of October 1871 and was rebuilt the next year, and the second, raised at St. Louis in 1869, covers an acre with wards for the insane, nervous diseases, and inebriety. Bishop Vaughan of Salford invited the brothers to England in June 1875, and the Bishop of Middlesborough brought them to his diocese in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algonquins:
The Algonquins were probably once the largest North American tribes, roaming between Kentucky and Hudson Bay, and between the Atlantic and the Mississippi, perhaps further still. Shifting homes, marriages, alliances, captive-taking, and desertion blur tribal limits. Micmacs, Chippewas, Sacs, Illinois, Pequods, and Lenapes count among them, sharing language and build.

Eliot and Mather thought them utterly savage, while early French missionaries praised their minds, poetry, oratory, nobility, and even hand skill. Drake largely shares that view for Lake Superior Algonquins. Algonquin seems a general name, not a compact, permanent league like the Iroquois.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-horns:
Altar horns were four projections, one at each corner, on the Jewish altar. The projections gave the ancient altar its horned corners, a feature the Christian altar did not keep. Christian altars lack them, but cornu, Latin for horn, still names the altar's sides and corners. Cornu epistolae and cornu evangelii mean the epistle and gospel sides.

Cornu anterius and cornu posterius evangelii, or dexterum anterius and dexterum posterius, name the front or back corner on the gospel side. The old temple terms thus survive as a precise shorthand for positions around the Christian altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-lantern:
Altar lanterns shield altar candles and lamp from draughts, made of perforated metalwork or set with crystals. A lantern's closed sides still let the flame show while breaking the wind. They also accompany the Blessed Sacrament carried between altars, or as Viaticum to the sick. For processions within the church they top high staves; for Viaticum a ring tops them, carried in a cleric's or assistant's hand.

These modest guards keep the light alive where draughts would kill an open flame, in church and on the road to the sick.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-linens:
The altar linens are the corporal, pall, purificator, and finger towels. The Blessed Sacrament and its vase must always rest on a corporal of linen or hemp, without embellishment or embroidery. Fine lace edges and a cross near the front edge are allowed, none in the centre. Muslin and cotton corporals are forbidden.

The pall began as part of the oversized corporal itself, only later becoming distinct. The purificator, pure white linen or hemp, cleanses the chalice, its size unprescribed. Finger towels, used at the Lavabo and after Communion, may be any material, preferably linen or hemp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalricians:
The Amalricians were a heretical sect founded late in the twelfth century by Amaury de Bène of Chartres, cleric and Paris professor who died between 1204 and 1207. They professed a species of pantheism: God and the universe are one, God is everything and everything is God. That principle led them to deny Transubstantiation, confound good and evil as equally of God, and reject morality's laws, with peculiar views on the Trinity besides.

Many priests and clerics spread the errors undetected for a time, until principals and proselytes were arrested. A Paris council of bishops and doctors in 1210 pardoned ignorant converts. It imprisoned four principals for life, and burned ten obstinate priests and clerics after public degradation. The sect's end thus came by council, prison, and fire, its founder dead years before yet condemned with his disciples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-berna:
Ambrose Bernard O'Higgins, born in County Meath in 1720, died at Lima on 18 March 1810. Schooled at Cadiz through a priest uncle, he went to South America. He peddled at Lima, contracted roads, then joined the Spanish army's engineers. Rapid promotion brought nobility as Count of Bellenar, then Marquis of Orsorno with Chile's governorship in 1788, and in 1796 Peru's viceroyalty, ending with his death.

His only son Bernard, born at Chillán on 20 August 1776, died at Lima on 14 October 1842. Schooled in England from fifteen, he returned to Chile, joined the revolution as militia colonel, and mainly won Chacabuco on 12 February 1817, breaking Spain's power in Chile. Proclaimed Dictator after the capital's capture, he ruled ably for six years until a fickle populace deposed him in February 1823.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosians:
St. Ambrose founded no religious order, though he watched monastic beginnings in his diocese and provided for monks outside the episcopal city under one of his priests, as Augustine's Confessions tell. The first Ambrosian order began in woodland near Milan. Alexander Grivelli, Antonio Petrasancta, and Albert Besuzzi, three noble Milanese, sought retreat there. Other solitaries and priests joined them, with Gregory XI giving Augustine's Rule and special rules.

St. Charles Borromeo, reforming Milan under Trent, founded the Oblates of St. Ambrose in August 1578, endowing them with diocesan livings and part of the dissolved Humiliati's goods. In the nineteenth century, Poitiers's Bishop Pie and Paderborn's Bishop Martin followed Charles's example with priestly societies on Milanese Oblate lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-american-indi:
The American Indians entry surveys the native peoples: race type, origin, languages, houses, food, animals, industries, games, war, social order, religion, and burial. Physically the type shows brown skin, dark brown eyes, high cheek bones, straight black hair, and scant beard, colour varying from very light to almost black, not red as supposed. Origins assigned include Europe via Greenland or Atlantis, but Asia via Bering Straits has more advocates and reasons.

Religiously the Indian was an animist, every animal, plant, and object holding a spirit to propitiate or fear, sun, buffalo, and eagle among the most powerful. Burial varied by tribe and place, inhumation most widespread, Hurons and Iroquois letting bodies decay on scaffolds before gathering bones to a common place. Population collapse marks the later record. The Pawnee fell from 10,000 in 1838 to 650, the Kansas from 1,500 to 200.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amiens:
Amiens, ancient Ambianum, covers the Somme department, suffragan of Reims under the old regime, of Paris from 1802 to 1822, and of Reims again since 1822. Duchesne denies value to the two-St.-Firmin legend, an eighth-century tissue of incoherences. He holds Eulogius, defender of Christ's divinity in mid-fourth-century councils, the first bishop known to history. Later bishops include Charlemagne's Jessé, deposed under Louis the Pious, and William of Mâcon, Paris University's greatest jurist. Jean de Lagrange, the Amiens Cardinal of the Great Schism, François Faure, converter of Montausier and James II, and Bombelles, bishop from 1819 to 1822, follow.

The thirteenth-century cathedral is an admirable Gothic monument, studied carefully by Ruskin in his Bible of Amiens. Its nave is considered the ideal Gothic type.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ammonian-sect:
The Ammonian sections are marginal divisions of the four Gospels in nearly all Greek and Latin manuscripts, about 1,165 in number. Matthew takes 355, Mark 235, Luke 343, and John 232, varying slightly by manuscript. Until recently they were commonly believed devised by Ammonius of Alexandria about 220, with a now-lost Gospel Harmony. He was said to divide the Gospels into small numbered sections, similar where narratives run parallel. The last three Gospels' sections, or their numbers with evangelists' names, stood in parallel columns opposite Matthew's.

Eusebius's letter to Carpianus, however, restricts Ammonius's work to placing the last three Gospels' parallels alongside Matthew's text. The sections once once credited to Ammonius, now ascribed to Eusebius, who lived 265 to 340. The Harmony of Ammonius thus suggested the system, but Eusebius owns the sections as now known.

chapters-of-opera-being-historical-and-c:
Chapters of Opera, by Henry Edward Krehbiel, records the lyric drama in New York from its earliest days to the author's present. Krehbiel, musical editor of the New York Tribune, explains in his preface that the season of 1907-08 completed the Metropolitan Opera House's first twenty five years. Through that whole period he occupied the same reviewer's stall, D-15 on the ground floor, and this book is built from what he heard there.

Thirteen chapters of observations mix history, criticism, and personal record: companies, singers, conductors, and the long fight to give New York a permanent opera house. Krehbiel dedicates the volume to his wife Marie and daughter Helen, who shared many of the experiences described. Readers of his earlier Book of Operas get the companion piece here, less about plots than about performances, and about one critic's quarter century in the same seat.

commentary-on-the-epistle-to-the-galatia:
Martin Luther's Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, from his 1535 lectures, appears here in Theodore Graebner's translation for a 1937 American edition. Graebner's preface recounts publisher Zondervan's condition: he would streamline Luther into American speech, since Luther remains the greatest name in Protestantism, or not publish at all. The lectures expound Paul's letter verse by verse.

Luther's theme is justification by faith against the law's proper uses: the law serves a civil purpose and drives transgressors to grace, but must not step out of character into Christ's place. The commentary's warmth and combat made it Luther's own favorite of his works. Readers meet the reformer teaching students, not debating popes, in these pages.

early-plays-catiline-the-warrior-s-barro:
Henrik Ibsen's Early Plays gathers Catiline, The Warrior's Barrow and Olaf Liljekrans, translated from Norwegian by Anders Orbeck. The volume belongs to the Scandinavian Classics series, founded in the belief that familiarity with northern literature would help Americans understand Scandinavians.

Ibsen himself insisted that his dramas were not isolated accidents, and the introduction stresses the orderly development of his genius from these early works onward. Catiline shows the young Ibsen already wrestling with rebellion and fate, while the other plays display his romantic, national phase. edison-his-life-and-inventions:
Frank Lewis Dyer, general counsel for the Edison laboratory, and Thomas Commerford Martin, past president of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote this authorized life of Thomas Edison. The contents run from the age of electricity and Edison's pedigree through his Port Huron boyhood and telegraph years. Boston, the stock ticker, and quadruplex telegraphy follow.

Later chapters cover the phonograph, the long hunt for lamp filament, Menlo Park memories, and the building of a complete lighting system. The authors had Edison's papers and cooperation, so technical claims come with inside detail. Their account of ore-concentrating work shows his optimism under staggering requirements. The biography remains a primary source on Edison's methods, if an admiring one.
eight-cousins:
Louisa May Alcott sent a delicate orphan to be raised by science and cousins in Eight Cousins. Rose Campbell, lately bereaved and brought up on salons and sickrooms, arrives at the Aunt Hill in Boston to live under her guardian, Uncle Alec, a sea-surgeon with theories. His prescription scandalizes the aunts: fresh air, plain food, loose dresses, work, and the company of her seven boy cousins, from steady Archie to baby Jamie.

Rose blooms under the regimen, and the cousins' scrapes and festivals fill the year. Alcott writes reform into a family story: health, dress, and girls' education argued through affection rather than lectures. Eight Cousins followed Little Women and shares its faith that love, properly administered, is a kind of medicine. Rose's progress from invalid to manager delights still.
eminent-victorians: Eminent Victorians, Lytton Strachey's famous biographical quartet. The debunking classic. This book preserves that biography. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Kept for readers. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
evergreens:
Jerome K Jerome begins Evergreens by pitying the shrubs of his title, so dull beside snowdrops, crocuses, and summer roses. Evergreens stand cold and hard while everything else puts on gladness, he writes, and seem dowdier as the garden brightens. The image becomes a way into memory, youth, and the people who stay faithful out of season.

The sketches drift from garden meditation to remembered scrapes, including two proud young men trapped in an undignified position and unwilling to call the family down for help. Jerome mixes the joke with genuine sentiment about spring and lost years. Readers who like his gentle, wandering essays will find the evergreen a fitting emblem for his tone.
fast-in-the-ice-adventures-in-the-polar-: Fast in the Ice, adventures in the polar regions, by R, m, ballantyne, the arctic tale. This book preserves that adventure. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
flatland-a-romance-of-many-dimensions:
Edwin Abbott Abbott, an English schoolmaster and church scholar, wrote Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions in 1884. He published it under the name of its hero, A Square. The hero lives in Flatland, a world of two dimensions. There men are shapes with many sides, and women are straight lines. Rank follows geometry in a strict social ladder.

A Square dreams of one-dimensional Lineland. Then a Sphere from three-dimensional Spaceland visits him. The Sphere lifts him out of his world to see it from above. Back home, no one will believe him. He is jailed for preaching a third dimension. Abbott mixes math with satire of Victorian class and sex roles. The tale also puzzles over how hard it is to picture what lies past our own senses.
ghazali-confessions:
Al-Ghazali, the great Muslim thinker of Baghdad, wrote his Deliverance from Error near the end of his life, around 1100. Claude Field's version appeared under the title The Confessions of Al-Ghazzali. Ghazali had been the most famous teacher in Baghdad.

He tells how doubt about all knowledge drove him to quit his post and wander. Years of Sufi practice, he says, gave him the certainty that books could not. The short work reshaped Islamic theology and is still read as a classic of spiritual searching. Many call it the finest autobiography in medieval Islam.
govdocs-archive_org-fer-latin-american-l:
Knights of Lucifer gathers Latin American luciferian and Hyperborean writings by several hands, including L. Wotan, Ignacio Ondargain, Piedra Iberica, Orlando Croy Romero, and Geburah Michel Lycanon. The compilation comes from the esoteric underground of the Spanish-speaking world.

The pieces treat Lucifer as a bringer of light and a rebel against the Christian order, mixed with Hyperborean myth about a lost northern homeland. Such texts circulate in small esoteric circles rather than through bookshops. The collection is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a sample of that Latin American fringe literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationsR: nsia-AssassinationsRacist Assassinations De Gaulle CIA: the made public government document on killing plots against de Gaulle and the CIA's role. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIACubans_CIA_C: Myra MacPherson, an Associated Press writer, titled her piece on the Bay of Pigs' long aftermath The Last Casualty of the Bay of Pigs. The failed 1961 invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained exiles left prisoners and widows. It left a wound in Cuban-American politics that lasted decades, and MacPherson's article returns to that aftermath. It is preserved as a single article among the archive's CIA and Cuba clippings, from the years when the invasion's story was still being settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FensterwaldBern:
Joseph Berger wrote about a new book on the Kennedy assassination by Bernard Fensterwald, titled Coincidence or Conspiracy. Fensterwald built his book around three people. Each of the three had intriguing encounters with both Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby, the two men at the center of the Dallas story.

A book built on such crossings invites readers to judge the pattern for themselves. Coincidence or planned connection is the question the title poses. Berger's article presents the book and its three figures to readers weighing that question, part of the large literature the assassination produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Mexican-America:
Peter Nabokov reported for the Washington Post on December 16, 1968, that Reies Lopez Tijerina had been acquitted. Tijerina led a land-grant movement in New Mexico. The charges grew out of a 1967 raid on a courthouse, in which his followers went looking for a district attorney they meant to arrest.

The raid made Tijerina a national figure in the Chicano movement. His acquittal, on the charges Nabokov covers, was a courtroom victory after a trial that drew wide attention. The article records the verdict and the reaction of officials, who were stunned by it. It preserves a turning point in a movement that tied modern protest to old Spanish land grants.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewOrleansExcha:
Chris Shearouse wrote about Exchange Alley in New Orleans, in an article titled 'Change in Exchange: Dilemma in an Alley.' The alley was born in 1831 as Exchange Passage. Shearouse covers the debate over its future: what to keep, what to change, and who decides.

Old alleys in the French Quarter carry two centuries of commerce in a few yards of brick. Articles like this one appear when a landmark's fate is argued in public. Shearouse gives the alley's history and the present dispute together. The piece is local journalism about preservation, filed in these papers because the alley also belongs to the Oswald story's New Orleans geography.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_CDC:
Starting in Havana, American diplomats began reporting strange illnesses with no clear cause. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spent two years on an epidemiologic investigation of those incidents. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted in February 2021, on the CDC report.

The report left the medical mystery unresolved, as the posting's title says. That non-answer is itself the news: a long, formal study could not settle what hurt the diplomats. Readers interested in the Havana Syndrome debate get the government's own investigative record rather than rumor or press summary.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
The National Security Act of 1947 built the machinery of modern American power. Rachel Santarsiero compiled this briefing book, number 799, published in July 2022 for the law's seventy-fifth anniversary. The statute established the CIA and the National Security Council.

It also laid the foundations of the Department of Defense. The posting calls the law's effect a complete overhaul of the executive branch. It transformed how foreign policy was made and powered America's global engagement through the Cold War and beyond. Anyone reading declassified records works inside institutions this single act created, which makes its anniversary set a useful map of the whole system.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_COU:
A new documentary film, COUP 53, examines the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, posted in August 2020, around a startling item the film features. It is a recently recovered interview with a former MI6 operative.

In that interview, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service is tied to the 1953 kidnapping of Tehran's chief of police. A kidnapping of the capital's police chief was no side detail in a coup; it removed a man who could have resisted. The posting links film research with the declassified record, each strengthening the other.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Doc:
Relations between Iran and the United States from 1978 to 2015 fill this National Security Archive collection. Those years run from the last period of the Shah's rule, through the revolution and hostage crisis, to the nuclear deal era. A documentary set spanning that whole arc is rare.

Most accounts treat those decades as separate stories: revolution, war, sanctions, talks. A single collection lets readers trace the same two governments across all of them. The value is continuity. Claims made in one decade can be checked against the paper of the next, which is exactly what a relations archive should allow.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
When Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Boris Yeltsin's Russia was the new partner the United States had to learn to work with. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book covers the first six months of that relationship. It is built on declassified records of the summits the two presidents held at Vancouver and in Tokyo that year.

The records show joint diplomatic work and a strikingly personal element: Clinton backed Yeltsin directly in his fight with the Russian parliament. That support helped set the tone for years of American policy toward Moscow. For readers, the papers capture a brief season when Washington treated Russia's shaky new democracy as a project worth personal risk from an American president.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_chile-cold-war-he:
Henry Kissinger shaped American foreign policy in the 1970s, and few figures of that era draw stronger praise or sharper blame. Under the heading Power by Any Means Necessary, the National Security Archive assembled a declassified dossier on his record. It is drawn from the secret files of the governments he dealt with, and of the one he served.

A dossier built from declassified papers lets readers test the legend against the memos. Kissinger, often shortened to HAK in the files of the time, left an unusually full paper trail across wars, coups, and secret diplomacy. The collection's value is that it argues with documents rather than opinion, giving critics and defenders alike the same evidence to work from.
graded-lessons-in-english-an-elementary-:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg's Graded Lessons in English is an elementary English grammar, famous for its sentence diagrams. The book teaches pupils to analyse sentences by placing words on a heavy horizontal line for the main clause, with vertical, diagonal and dotted lines for modifiers and subordinate parts.

Lessons proceed step by step, so that a child learns parts of speech, sentence structure and correct usage together, rather than by rote rules alone. Generations of American schoolchildren learned grammar from Reed and Kellogg, and their diagrams became a classroom institution. Teachers and historians of education will find this volume the classic statement of the diagramming method.
happy-hawkins:
Robert Alexander Wason put a cowboy at the center of Happy Hawkins and let him tell the tale in dialect. Happy, born in Indiana, ran west as a boy hunting Indians and found hunger instead. Lunch counters, silent ranch bosses, and open ranges school him. His nickname fits: humor carries him through work, fights, and love alike.

The Diamond Dot ranch gives the story its home ground across thirty chapters. Happy convinces a cook, rides under fire, sets a broken leg, and drifts off whenever restlessness calls. A lasso duel, a winter at Slocum's Luck, and questions over Chinese labor mark the middle episodes. Barbie, the ranch girl, slowly turns the comedy toward courtship, discovery, and a wedding day. A final reckoning and an afterglow chapter close the wanderer's account. Western readers who like talk, ranch routine, and a soft heart under the slang will enjoy Happy's company.
human-nature-and-other-sermons:
Joseph Butler, Bishop of Durham, preached the sermons gathered in this Cassell volume of 1887, and the introduction gives his life from his birth at Wantage in 1692. Butler argued his way from a Presbyterian upbringing into the Church of England, took his Oxford degree, and in 1718 became preacher at the Rolls Chapel in London. The sermons on human nature that open the book were preached there.

Butler's argument in those sermons is moral anatomy. Human nature is a system of appetites, affections, self-love, benevolence, and, ruling over all, conscience. Self-love and benevolence are not enemies; each passion has its proper object and place. The later sermons take up charity, resentment, and the love of God. Few English sermons have been argued over so long by philosophers.
hunted-down-the-detective-stories-of-cha:
Charles Dickens opens Hunted Down, his 1860 detective tale, through a retired life assurance manager who claims to have seen more romances in thirty years of business than most men. A smooth client named Slinkton wins his trust, then suspicion, as a young lady's death and an insurance policy come together. The manager sets himself to hunt the man down.

A drunken associate named Beckwith, brandy saucepan in hand, becomes an unlikely instrument of exposure. Dickens builds the short novel from office observation rather than police procedure, making the detective an amateur of character. This edition, from Hard Times and Reprinted Pieces, collects Dickens's contributions to crime writing, a field his Inspector Bucket had already transformed.
indian-heroes-and-great-chieftains:
Charles A. Eastman, a Dakota Sioux doctor and writer known also as Ohiyesa, wrote Indian Heroes and Great Chieftains, published in 1919. Eastman profiles the Native leaders he most admired, telling their lives from inside the world that produced them. His pages carry Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse of the Sioux, Red Cloud, Spotted Tail, and Little Crow.

He crosses the continent for others: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, Geronimo of the Apache, and the Shawnee and Sac and Fox leaders of older wars. Eastman writes as a bridge figure, educated in white schools yet loyal to his people's honor. The book set out to give young readers, Native and white alike, heroes told truly, and it still reads with quiet force.
intentions:
Oscar Wilde gathered his four great critical dialogues and essays as Intentions, first published in 1891 and reprinted by Methuen in 1913. The Decay of Lying opens the book in a Nottinghamshire library, where Vivian argues that art should not copy life because life copies art. Cyril plays the straight man and loses beautifully.

Pen, Pencil, and Poison studies the forger Wainewright as an artist in crime. The Critic as Artist, the longest piece, claims criticism is itself creative, and The Truth of Masks defends costume and paradox in Shakespeare. Wilde's epigrams here became the doctrine of the aesthetic movement, argued with a learning that keeps surprising readers who expected only wit.
jan-of-the-windmill-a-story-of-the-plain:
Jan of the Windmill, a story of the plains by Juliana Horatia Ewing, follows a baby left with a miller's family and raised beside the sails. Ewing's tale appears here in a fifth edition from London, dated 1890, with eleven illustrations by Helen Paterson Allingham. The contents promise a windmiller's wife, strangers at the mill, and a payment of ten shillings a week for the little Jan.

Chapter headings trace the boy's growing up in plain village terms. He works as a nurse boy, minds pigs, and learns beside Abel, the miller's man, who plays schoolmaster over a spelling column. A pocket book and a family Bible carry a five pound reward and a buried question about his birth. Visitors bring a tiny lady with a grand name and a cure for whooping cough. Kindness, class, and a foundling's secret carry the story.
jimmie-higgins:
Jimmie Higgins is a novel by Upton Sinclair, the American writer known for exposing social wrongs. Its contents page alone maps Jimmie's whole path in twenty chapter titles. He meets a candidate, hears a speech, and debates the issue. Then he strikes it rich, helps the Kaiser, and goes to jail.

Later chapters send Jimmie back to nature, face to face with an owner, and into open war. He meets a patriot, dodges trouble, and takes the road. The titles then turn sharp: Jimmie turns Bolshevik, meets a tempter, and wrestles with him. At last he takes the plunge and puts on khaki. Sinclair builds a working man's political education into a story.
journals-of-australian-explorations:
Journals of Australian Explorations gathers the expedition journals of Augustus Charles Gregory and his brother Francis Thomas Gregory. Both men were fellows of the Royal Geographical Society and gold medalists of it. The Brisbane government printer issued the volume in 1884. Its preface explains that readers kept asking for journals long out of print.

Earlier, the journals had appeared only in fragments. This volume collects them whole, for reference and for the permanent record. It leaves the brothers' first impressions unchanged, even where later knowledge corrected them. The first journal covers the 1846 expedition east and north of Swan River. A settlers' expedition under A. C. Gregory in 1848 follows. Together they trace early attempts to open Australia's unknown interior.
judith-of-the-plains:
Judith of the Plains is a novel by Marie Manning, published by Harper and Brothers in 1903. Twenty chapters carry the story, opening simply with Town. Judith works as postmistress, as one chapter title announces. Leander and his lady, the Rodneys at home, and Mrs. Yellett and her 'government' fill the early cast.

The plot moves onto the horse-thief trail and into a cabin in the valley. A round-up, a wolf hunt, and the land of the red silence follow. Mary spends her first day in camp, and Judith adjusts the situation. Cloudburst, hanging threats, and a final ball close the contents. Manning writes a Western of ranch life with a capable heroine at its center.
keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-plains:
Keith of the Border: A Tale of the Plains is a Western novel by Randall Parrish. Thirty-six chapters carry it from The Plainsman to The End. Early chapters stage a sudden arrest and a desperate escape. A ride through sand and desert leads to a wilderness cabin and the girl there.

Keith crosses the ford of the Arkansas and reaches the marshal of Sheridan. Christie Maclaire enters as one who believes in him, and a message from the dead complicates his case. An Indian raid, a duel in the desert, and a single shot raise the stakes. The final chapters bring forgiveness and a last interview. Parrish writes fast frontier adventure around a wronged plainsman clearing his name.
life-of-charles-dickens:
Frank T. Marzials wrote this Dickens life for the Great Writers series. Walter Scott published it in London in 1887. Marzials acknowledges a heavy debt to Forster's life of Dickens. He also used the letters edited by Dickens's family.

Charles Dickens was born on February 7, 1812. Happy Chatham days gave way to family troubles and London hardship. His father entered the Marshalsea, and Charles worked in a blacking business. Marzials compares the boy's isolation with David Copperfield's story. Kitton's Dickensiana lightened Marzials's labor considerably, he acknowledges. Young Charles felt isolation keenly during the blacking warehouse months.
lives-of-the-three-mrs-judsons:
Arabella M. Willson wrote these lives of three missionary wives. Ann, Sarah, and Emily Judson each married the same missionary. All three served as missionaries to Burmah in turn. Lee and Shepard published the book in Boston.

Congress copyright records date its entry to 1855. Portraits of Ann and Emily Judson illustrate the volume. A verse epigraph praises their self-denying band of workers. They counted life cheap to fulfil their ministry, it says. Miller, Orton and Mulligan first entered the copyright in 1855. Charles Dillingham later sold the New York edition.
love-among-the-chickens:
Love Among the Chickens is an early comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse. In his dedication, Wodehouse thanks his friend W. Townend for giving him the stuff. Sixteen years before, he says, they were sprightly lads at school together. The stuff Townend gave him became a chicken farm by the sea.

A young writer joins his friend's hopeless chicken venture on the coast. Hens, eggs, and farm chaos fill the days there. Amid the squawking, the young man falls in love. Wodehouse keeps the tone light, bright, and full of jokes. The book shows his high spirits long before his fame peaked. It is vintage early Wodehouse, warm and very funny.
men-like-gods-dover-thrift-editions:
H. G. Wells published this utopian novel in 1923. Its hero, Mr. Barnstaple, is a tired journalist who takes a holiday drive in 1921. He and several other motorists are suddenly swept three thousand years into the future. This Dover edition reprints the original Macmillan text.

The travelers land in a world remade along Barnstaple's own ideals. Crime, poverty, war, disease, and bigotry have all vanished there. Wells uses the visit to test his hopes for science and social planning. The novel asks whether ordinary modern people could bear such a perfected world, or would spoil it.
missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-indian:
The Reverend Edward F. Wilson tells here how he came to work among the Ojibway of Canada. His contents trace the journey: first experiences, arrival at Sarnia, and work at Kettle Point. He records Indian names given to the missionaries and a Christmas spent on the reserve. The bishop's visit and a first trip to Garden River follow.

Later chapters describe baptisms of pagan Indians and the Red River expedition. Wilson meets Chief Little Pine and winters in Algoma. His account preserves detail about Ojibway life, language, and customs in his era. Mission memoirs like his remain sources, read critically, for nineteenth-century Indigenous history around the Great Lakes.
modern-italian-poets-essays-and-versions:
William Dean Howells wrote these essays on Italy's modern poets, adding his own English versions of their verse. The contents begin with the Arcadian shepherds of the eighteenth century. Giuseppe Parini, Vittorio Alfieri, and Vincenzo Monti follow. Ugo Foscolo and Alessandro Manzoni anchor the Romantic generation.

Howells gives Giacomo Leopardi a place among the later names. Giuseppe Giusti, Giovanni Prati, and Aleardo Aleardi continue the line to his own century. Silvio Pellico, famous for his prison memoir, appears as a poet here. Howells, America's leading novelist-critic of his day, introduced English readers to Italian poetry he had loved since his consulate at Venice.
more-toasts-jokes-stories-and-quotations:
Marion Dix Mosher, a Rochester public librarian, compiled this handbook in 1922. The H. W. Wilson Company published it at New York. At 552 pages it promises jokes, stories, and quotations for speakers. The contents open with an essay on the importance of humor.

That essay, reprinted from the Nineteenth Century, calls humor a divine gift. It deals, the essay says, with a mystery pleasantly woven into daily life. Toasts fill the body of the book, with an index for finding them fast. Banquet speakers and toastmasters of the 1920s kept such compilations at hand, and librarians like Mosher built them for reference shelves.
mother-carey-s-chickens:
Kate Douglas Wiggin opens this family story with the petrels called Mother Carey's chickens. The birds flit from wave to wave like swallows over the sea. Mother Carey herself heads the first chapter, and her chickens the second. A chapter called The Common Denominator introduces the family's shared life.

Then comes The Broken Circle, and the Careys' flitting, or move, to Beulah. Cousin Ann, a service on the threshold, and a housewarming mark the new home. Nancy's idea and Nancy's coming out carry the eldest girl forward. Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes of a widowed mother holding her brood together with cheer.
my-literary-passions:
William Dean Howells maps his reading life in this 1895 book. The contents begin with the bookcase at home. Goldsmith, Cervantes, and Irving mark his early loves. First fiction and drama follow, then Scott and Pope.

Uncle Tom's Cabin, Ossian, and Shakespeare each get a chapter. Dickens, Thackeray, Dante, and Tolstoy mark later stages. He ends with new names like Zola, Hardy, and Galdos. Howells tells how each book formed his taste and craft. The memoir is a reader's autobiography, warm and exact, showing how one boy's shelf became an American man of letters.
nasa-tm-19650015349-1964-publications:
Compiled by the Materials Division at Marshall and dated January 30, 1965, this volume lists NASA publications from 1964. The entries are technical notes from across the agency's programs. Subjects run from materials and propulsion to spacecraft and engineering development work of many kinds.

A yearly list like this one served as a finding aid. Researchers could scan one volume to see what the agency had released. They could then order the notes that mattered to their own work.
